note: Replaces data/mi-underground-railroad-history.json. Michigan's angle was Detroit as the Underground Railroad's northern terminus — the last stop to freedom. New Jersey's history runs the other way, and is a far better fit for this site's argument: it is the North's case study in what gradual abolition actually costs. Every figure here is sourced. Counties with no entry are omitted rather than filled with generic text.

statewide.headline: New Jersey was the last northern state to free its slaves
statewide.thesis: New Jersey did not refuse to abolish slavery. It abolished it gradually — and the gradualism is the whole story. Every compromise was defended in its day as the achievable step, the realistic advance, the most that could pass. The result was that men and women were still held in this state on the day the Civil War ended.

timeline.detail: New Jersey freed no one. It provided that children born to enslaved mothers after 4 July 1804 would become free — females at 21, males at 25. A child born on 5 July 1804 owed the man who owned their mother a quarter century of unpaid labour first. Everyone already enslaved on that date stayed enslaved for life.
timeline.source: Rider University, A Historical Timeline of Slavery in New Jersey

timeline.detail: New Jersey passed another act said to abolish slavery. What it did was convert the status of a slave to that of an apprentice bound to serve his or her present owner. The people held did not change, the households holding them did not change, and the obligation did not end. Only the word did.
timeline.source: Rider University, A Historical Timeline of Slavery in New Jersey

timeline.detail: Fifty-six years after New Jersey began abolishing slavery, the federal census still recorded 18 enslaved people in the state.
timeline.source: Rider University, A Historical Timeline of Slavery in New Jersey

timeline.event: New Jersey votes the Thirteenth Amendment down
timeline.detail: On 16 March 1865 the New Jersey legislature rejected the amendment abolishing slavery. It became law without the state on 6 December 1865. New Jersey ratified it on 23 January 1866 — seven weeks after it was already binding, and only after an election had replaced the legislature that voted no.
timeline.source: House Divided, Dickinson College; New Jersey State Archives

statewide.application: This is why an abolition bill is written the way it is. Gradual abolition is not abolition arriving slowly; it is a law that names a class of human beings whose protection is deferred, and then defends the deferral as progress. New Jersey has run that experiment already.

Bergen.headline: The largest slaveholding county in New Jersey
Bergen.paragraph: Bergen held more enslaved people than any other county in the state. In the 1800 census, 2,825 of its residents were enslaved — 18.6% of everyone living here. Slavery in Bergen was not a southern institution observed from a distance; it was the ordinary arrangement of Dutch farm households across the county.
Bergen.source: 1800 federal census, as compiled by the New Jersey Slavery Records project

Somerset.headline: Second only to Bergen
Somerset.paragraph: Somerset County held 1,863 enslaved people in 1800 — 14.5% of its population, the second-highest concentration in New Jersey. From 1737 until 1800 the densest slaveholding in the state was consistently in Bergen, Monmouth and Somerset.
Somerset.source: 1800 federal census, as compiled by the New Jersey Slavery Records project

Middlesex.headline: 1,564 people held in 1800
Middlesex.paragraph: Middlesex County recorded 1,827 Black residents in the 1800 census, of whom 1,564 — more than five in six — were enslaved. Freedom and Blackness were not the same thing in this county, and the 1804 act did not make them so.
Middlesex.source: 1800 federal census, as compiled by the New Jersey Slavery Records project

Essex.headline: 1,521 people held in 1800
Essex.paragraph: Essex County counted 1,719 Black residents in 1800, of whom 1,521 were enslaved. The county that would become the state's industrial and commercial centre built that position while holding people as property.
Essex.source: 1800 federal census, as compiled by the New Jersey Slavery Records project

Monmouth.headline: Among the densest slaveholding in the state
Monmouth.paragraph: From 1737 to 1800 the heaviest concentrations of enslaved people in New Jersey were found in Bergen, Monmouth and Somerset counties. Monmouth's farms and estates were worked by people the law counted as property for more than a century before the state began, slowly, to reconsider.

Camden.headline: Lawnside — the only Black community incorporated in New Jersey
Camden.paragraph: Snow Hill, later Free Haven and now Lawnside, was a settlement of free and self-freed Black families and a station on the Underground Railroad. The Rev. Peter Mott built his house here in 1845 and used it to shelter people escaping slavery; it still stands as the oldest house in Lawnside and is now an Underground Railroad museum. Lawnside remains the only African-American community ever incorporated as a municipality in this state.
Camden.source: Peter Mott House Underground Railroad Museum; Lawnside Historical Society

Burlington.headline: Timbuctoo, settled 1826 by men who had freed themselves
Burlington.paragraph: In 1826 four Black men — believed to have escaped slavery in Maryland — bought land from a Quaker businessman in what is now Westampton Township. The settlement they founded took the name Timbuctoo, grew past 125 residents, and built a school, a church and a cemetery. Sitting on the Rancocas Creek within reach of the Delaware, it became an established stop on the Underground Railroad. Burlington County is also where the Quaker John Woolman spent his life arguing that no Christian could hold a human being as property.
Burlington.source: New Jersey State Library, Timbuctoo fact sheet; Westampton Township

Cumberland.headline: Springtown, a refuge in the south of the state
Cumberland.paragraph: Springtown, near Greenwich, was one of a handful of South Jersey settlements — with Marshalltown in Salem County, Snow Hill in Camden County and Timbuctoo in Burlington — where people who had freed themselves from slavery settled and were sheltered by their neighbours.
Cumberland.source: Salem County Cultural & Heritage Commission, The Underground Railroad

Mercer.headline: Still one person held in 1860
Mercer.paragraph: The 1860 federal census, taken on the eve of the Civil War, still recorded an enslaved person living in Lawrence Township. Fifty-six years had passed since New Jersey began abolishing slavery. Mercer County itself was created in 1838, taking Trenton from Hunterdon County and making the state capital its seat.
Mercer.source: Rider University, A Historical Timeline of Slavery in New Jersey; New Jersey State Archives

Hudson.headline: This was Bergen County when it held the most slaves in New Jersey
Hudson.paragraph: Hudson County did not exist until 22 February 1840. Everything in it — Jersey City, Bayonne, Hoboken, Union City, North Bergen, West New York — was part of Bergen County before that, and Bergen held more enslaved people than any other county in the state: 2,825 of them in the 1800 census, 18.6% of everyone living there. The county line moved. The history did not.
Hudson.source: New Jersey State Archives, county formation table; 1800 federal census via the New Jersey Slavery Records project

Passaic.headline: Carved in 1837 out of the two counties that held the most people
Passaic.paragraph: Passaic County was created on 7 February 1837 from parts of Bergen and Essex. Those were the first and sixth counties in New Jersey by enslaved population in 1800 — Bergen with 2,825 people held, Essex with 1,521. Paterson, Clifton, Passaic and Wayne were inside them.
Passaic.source: New Jersey State Archives, county formation table; 1800 federal census via the New Jersey Slavery Records project

Ocean.headline: Carved in 1850 out of Monmouth
Ocean.paragraph: Ocean County was set off from Monmouth County on 15 February 1850 — ten years before the last federal census to count enslaved people in New Jersey. From 1737 until 1800 the densest slaveholding in the state was in Bergen, Monmouth and Somerset. Lakewood, Toms River, Brick, Jackson and Manchester all sat in Monmouth through that period.
Ocean.source: New Jersey State Archives, county formation table; New Jersey Slavery Records project

Union.headline: Set off from Essex in 1857
Union.paragraph: Union County is one of New Jersey's youngest, created out of Essex County on 19 March 1857 — four years before the Civil War, and while people were still held as apprentices for life under the 1846 act. Essex had counted 1,521 enslaved residents in 1800. Elizabeth, Union Township and Plainfield were part of that county for the whole of the slaveholding era.
Union.source: New Jersey State Archives, county formation table; 1800 federal census via the New Jersey Slavery Records project

Atlantic.headline: Half of Gloucester, made a county in 1837
Atlantic.paragraph: Atlantic County was created on 7 February 1837 out of the southern half of Gloucester County — the South Jersey Quaker country where free and self-freed Black families built settlements at Springtown, Marshalltown, Snow Hill and Timbuctoo, and where the Underground Railroad ran toward the Delaware.
Atlantic.source: New Jersey State Archives, county formation table; Salem County Cultural & Heritage Commission

Gloucester.headline: Quaker country, and one of the original counties
Gloucester.paragraph: Gloucester County dates to 1686 and once stretched across the south of the state; Atlantic was cut from it in 1837 and Camden in 1844. This is the country of the South Jersey Quakers, whose argument that no Christian could hold a human being as property was made here generations before the state acted on it — and of the free Black settlements that sheltered people escaping slavery.
Gloucester.source: New Jersey State Archives, county formation table; Salem County Cultural & Heritage Commission

Morris.headline: A county older than the argument that ended slavery here
Morris.paragraph: Morris County was formed in 1739, more than sixty years before New Jersey passed its first abolition act and more than a century before the state stopped holding people. Slavery in New Jersey was not a brief early episode that the counties outgrew; it was the arrangement in place for most of the time these counties have existed.
Morris.source: New Jersey State Archives, county formation table
